title: L5 Capstone: Mini Database
story: You just built a database! Not a toy — a real, working, in-memory database. It stores data, you can query it with conditions, update records, delete them, and list everything. Every major software system has a database at its core, and now you understand exactly how they work — because you built one from scratch using the collections you mastered.
why: Building a mini database synthesizes every L5 concept — structs, enums, Vec, Map, generics, and contracts — into a single working system that mirrors how real databases store and query data.
analogy: Your mini database is like a filing cabinet — each drawer is a Table, each folder in the drawer is a Row, and each field on the folder is a column-value pair. You just built the software version of that cabinet, and now you can open any drawer, find any folder, read it, update it, or toss it — all through code.
try_it: Add sorting: `Table.order_by(t: &Table, column: Str) -> Vec[Row]` that sorts rows by a numeric column value (convert string to int for comparison). Add pagination: `Table.get_page(t: &Table, page: Int, size: Int) -> Vec[Row]`. Add a `Database` type that holds multiple Tables in a Map[Str, Table]. Allow querying across tables: 'find all users in NYC who are over 25'. You've just built a query engine!
tips: A Row is just a Map[Str, Str] — every value is a string, which means you need to parse for numeric comparisons
Find_by scans every row (O(n)) — real databases use indexes (like a second Map) for faster queries
Delete operations return the count of removed rows — always tell the caller what happened
common_mistakes: Forgetting that all values are strings — comparing '10' == '10' works, but '10' > '5' compares alphabetically ('1' < '5'), not numerically
Modifying rows during iteration — build a new Vec for delete/filter operations, then replace the original
Not handling missing columns — `row.get(&column)` returns None if the column doesn't exist; default to ""
